# ‘Influencing the influencers’: Exploring the impact of an in-person summit on TikTokers’

# mental health communication habits and

# beliefs

Abstract Social media platforms such as TikTok hold tremendous promise for reaching large proportions

of the general population with health messaging. However, the proliferation of health

misinformation on these platforms poses a significant public health risk. Partnerships between

public health experts and social media content creators are a novel intervention which may

overcome concerns about misinformation and catalyze the proliferation of evidence-based

health messages on social media. To build such partnerships between creators and mental

health and health communication experts, The Center for Health Communication (CHC) at the

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health held an in-person summit that attracted mental

health creators working on TikTok and other social media platforms. Over the course of two

days, creators were exposed to techniques for communicating evidence-based research and

recommendations that promote mental health. Following the summit, creators who attended

the summit were re-contacted for in-depth interviews to assess the summit's impact on their

beliefs and behaviors. Results reveal that attending the summit changed creators’

content-making behaviors, increased their sense of responsibility and awareness of their power

to impact mental health outcomes among social media users, validated their work and

motivation as health communicators, and created a much-needed community of support

among peers. Given that social media is a primary source of health information for many

people, our findings provide a blueprint for public health communicators hoping to build lasting

strategic relationships with today’s most influential media gatekeepers.

## Introduction


<!-- Page 3 -->


Data from the US Centers for Disease Control’s National Health Interview Survey show that 6 in

10 U.S. adults use the internet to look for health information (Wang et al. 2023). Among

internet sources, social media platforms are an increasingly important source of health

information (Chen et al. 2021). The health information people find on social media platforms

can influence individuals’ health beliefs, their health behaviors, and whether they decide to

seek health care (Chen et al. 2018; Iftikhar et al., 2017).

But the quality of health information consumers find on these platforms is highly variable. Of

particular concern is the prevalence of health misinformation, including anecdotal information

(Afful-Dadzie et al., 2021), information not grounded in scientific evidence (Suarez-Lledo et al.,

2021), and commercial biases (Robbins et al, 2023).

Much of the health information on social media comes from individual creators who produce

and share video and image content. A subset of these creators have attracted large, loyal

communities that look to them for information and solidarity. Approximately 40% of

Americans—including 72% of those between the ages of 18 and 29—follow at least one content

creator on social media (Faverio & Anderson, 2022). In some cases, content creators have

developed credibility and trust with their audience sufficient to drive consumer behavior

(Kanaveedu et al., 2022).

Health communicators have begun exploring how creators’ work might also influence

population health. For example, digital campaigns that partner with social media content

creators for additional reach have successfully influenced healthy behavior such as smoking

cessation (Kostigana et al., 2020). Studies have also shown that content from influential content

creators has been shown to increase audiences’ knowledge and positive attitudes about

vaccines (Bonnevie et al., 2020). Further, research has found that when celebrities or other

influential figures share their mental health struggles on social media, doing so can reduce

stigma and enhance public awareness about the mental health conditions (Lee et al., 2021;

Lotun et al., 2022).


<!-- Page 4 -->


But other studies have shown that creators’ work can also negatively affect population health,

for example, by encouraging tobacco use (Lim et al., 2024) or spreading health misinformation

(Mututwa et al., 2020; Robbins et al., 2023).

Given the amount of health misinformation now circulating on social media platforms, there is a

pressing need for research into how public health might influence more creators to spread

evidence-based content on social platforms—and protect the health of their digital

communities (Pretorius et al., 2019). This is especially critical considering that creators on these

platforms are deeply engaging those that public health and mainstream media often struggle to

reach, including young people, Black people, Hispanic people, and those from other

marginalized backgrounds (Auxier & Anderson, 2021). Moreover, young people increasingly

consider social media and the creators that work on these platforms trusted sources of health

information (Liedke & Gottfried, 2022; Montera et al., 2024).

As a result of this need, researchers have begun to conduct interventional research to see how

public health institutions can influence social media creators' content. In one example, our team

embedded a rigorous randomized controlled trial in a field experiment on TikTok to explore how

exposure to digital toolkits and/or virtual training can influence creators to spread

evidence-based mental health information. We found that creators exposed to the toolkits were

more likely to share evidence from the toolkits on TikTok the month after the intervention

(Motta et al., 2024).

To explore what impacts, if any, an in-person intervention might have on creators, we created a

2-day summit for mental health creators, which included training in mental health research and

health communication strategies. Providing in-person training in science communication best

practices to journalists working in traditional media has been shown to have lasting impacts on

journalists’ beliefs and behaviors, making them both more likely to report a greater sense of

efficacy (Smith & Morgoch, 2022) and more likely incorporate more scientific material overall,

and peer-reviewed studies and scientists’ quotes in particular (Smith et al., 2024). In this study,

we explore what impacts, if any, our summit had on the health communication beliefs and

behaviors of creators working in social media.


<!-- Page 5 -->


Although journalists’ role in ensuring access to public health information is well established,

creators’ role in such is far less so. So we also explore whether creators exposed to this

intervention might be more likely to see themselves as part of the public health communication,

have a lasting impact on their use of evidence-based information in their videos and look for

ways to collaborate with researchers and other experts.

Although to our knowledge, the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health [institute blinded for

review] is the first public health institution to organize an in-person summit between social

media content creators and researchers, others have argued that creator-researcher

partnerships are needed for wide and equitable dissemination of science and health

information (Galetti & Costa-Pereira, 2017). This study aims to help the health communication

community better understand how to design creator-public health programs that can improve

and protect the health information on social media, an increasingly important social

determinant of health.

## Methods

Study design

This study is an extension of a prior TikTok field study of social media creators (Motta et al.,

2024). In that initial study, the team collaborated with 42 prominent content creators who met

their selection criteria; namely, individuals aged 18 or over who produce English-language

mental health content, have at least 10,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram social media

platforms, post at least 4 times per month on TikTok, had been active on the platform for at

least one year and posted no red flags, defined as harmful, misleading or otherwise problematic

content.

We then invited creators who had been randomly selected to receive virtual mental health

communication training and materials in that study to attend a in-person summit, during which


<!-- Page 6 -->


they 1) learned about mental health research, 2) received didactic instruction on health

communication techniques for disseminating evidence-based mental health information and 3)

networked with mental health experts and each other. Hereafter, this intervention will be

referred to as the summit.

We undertook a two-stage study to evaluate the impact of the summit, leveraging a post-event

survey administered to attendees to develop themes for subsequent qualitative interviews that

would explore the rich and varied experiences of creators who attended the summit. Similar

methods have been used, for example, to study the effect of training non-professionals to offer

peer mentoring on a digital mental health platform (McCosker, 2018).

This research was reviewed and approved by the Harvard Longwood Campus Institutional

Review Board, which deemed the study exempt from the need for full IRB review. All

participants were required to verbally state their informed consent before starting the interview

The participants were not financially compensated for their time.

Interview guide design

Responses to a post-summit survey administered from August 30th 2023 to September 6th

2023 informed the questions used in our interview guide (see Supplementary Material). In the

survey, creators were asked to offer open-ended responses to the following questions: “Has the

[in-person summit] changed how you think about creating mental health content? If so, how?”

And, “What did you find most useful about the [in-person summit]?” The responses, as well as

deductive codes informed by those responses, are outlined in full in the Results section.

Data collection

The post-summit survey was emailed to all participants. Recruitment for the qualitative

interviews was done via the summit organizer’s monthly creator community call, its creator

group text, its creator Slack channel, and via email. In each case, recruitment materials clearly

introduced the aim of the mental health communication study at Harvard Chan School. All


<!-- Page 7 -->


recruitment communications were conducted through the summit organizer’s official channels.

Recruitment materials are available in Supplementary Materials.

Data analysis

The interview transcripts were uploaded to the Delve qualitative data analysis software (Delve,

2024). The interviewer assigned each creator with a random number to maintain their

anonymity when studying their transcript. The lead author categorized segments of the

transcript into the deductive codes and generated additional inductive codes from analysis of

the transcripts, which were reviewed by a senior author. Additionally, the second author

reviewed the transcripts and the accuracy of the codes assigned. After the review, the first and

second authors met to resolve any discrepancies in selected codes. All codes were then

reviewed with a senior author and classified into broader themes. For example, codes about

creators' content decisions, such as “Use more citations/disclaimers” and “Use more scientific

language/framing in their content,” were combined to generate a theme about how the summit

affected creators’ content strategy. The analysis was grounded in constructivism, where the

authors study the meaning that participants attribute to their experience (Given, 2008).

## Results

Study sample

The summit was held August 3-4, 2023. The post-event survey, administered Aug 31, 2023

through September 6, 2023, was sent to all 14 creators who participated in the summit; 10 of

the 14 responded. Qualitative interviews were conducted March 19, 2024 through May 23,

2024; we reached out to all 14 creators and 79% (11 out of 14) participated.

All 11 creators interviewed are based in North America. Of those, 55% (n = 6) of the creators

self-identified as mental health clinicians, whereas the remainder create content based on their

lived experience with mental health. All 11 creators reported that they are active on TikTok and

Instagram. According to a review of their TikTok and Instagram channels, their collective reach


<!-- Page 8 -->


across these platforms totals more than 5.4 million. Their individual reach on these platforms

(TikTok + Instagram) ranges from 62,000 to 1,384,000. Other platforms on which they reported

being active include YouTube (n=7), Facebook (n = 3), and X (n=2); 5 also reported hosting a

podcast.

Results from post-summit survey (administered August 31, 2023 through September 6, 2023)

Creators were asked to rate from a scale of 1 to 5 (1- Strongly disagree, 2-Disagree, 3-Neither

agree nor disagree, 4-Agree, 5- Strongly agree) their agreement on each of three statements:

“The [in-person summit] provided me with new knowledge or information that will aid my work

as a mental health creator” garnered 10 responses with an average rating of 5/5. “The

[in-person summit] provided me with materials (messaging, sources, calls to action, creative)

that will aid my work as a mental-health creator” garnered 10 responses with an average rating

of 4.9/5. “After attending the [in-person summit], I am likely to look for ways to use and/or cite

scientific evidence in my content” garnered 10 responses with an average of 5/5. These

responses suggested that the in-person summit convinced creators of the importance of using

evidence-based information and that they believed we had provided them with the information

and tools on how to do so more effectively.

Creators’ responses to the open-ended portion of the survey showed that creators believed the

summit gave them new content they could use, taught them how to better frame their content,

and helped them understand how to search for evidence-based information to share with their

audiences. Their responses also revealed that the summit changed the way the creators viewed

their role in public health, heightened their sense of responsibility toward their audience, and

created a sense of community with their creator-peers. Participants also reported that the

experience showed them the value of interacting with public health experts.

Deductive codes generated from these responses (Table 1) informed the questions asked in our

subsequent semi-structured interviews.

The summit changed creators’ long-term content strategy

The interviews revealed that participation in the in-person summit inspired evidence-based

content practices. There are several sub-codes within this broader theme. First, the summit

convinced or reminded some creators to more routinely seek out scientific evidence when

planning and researching content. Creator 9 mentioned “I think [the summit] helped me get

back into a regular routine of writing long form pieces that were rooted in research.” Others

reported that they had begun looking more at evidence when planning content, such as “I'll

research it and then if it's not accurate, then I'll probably be like, Okay, maybe that's not a good

video to put out.”(Creator 1). The summit also changed where creators look for resources.

Creator 7 said “I think what [the summit] did was provide me with resources and more exciting

ways to seek out more research.” Some creators reported they were more likely to cite their

sources when making content. For example, Creator 8 mentioned the summit helped them “be

more intentional about leaving the citations.”

Second, several creators explained that the summit inspired them to be more thoughtful about

topic selection, framing, and word choice. Creators explained that they became more aware of

how to evaluate different sources and find evidence-based information. They also reported that

learning about new research expanded the topics they tackled and increased their curiosity to

search for new topics. Creator 7 noted that the summit “made me expand what I'm talking

about. I posted stuff that I maybe wouldn't have posted before.” A few creators mentioned that

it affected the language they use in their content; for example, Creator 3 said “I no longer use


<!-- Page 18 -->


language that is very emotionally driven. I'll use language that's very science driven or logic

[driven].” Finally, several creators noted they have started to experiment with one of the topics

covered in the summit, gain framing (Rothman & Salovey, 1997). For example, Creator 7 noted

“So instead of saying everybody avoids things that are anxious, frame it as how empowering it

can feel when you don't avoid things that make you anxious.”

Third, even though most creators reported sharing more evidence-based content as a result of

attending the in-person summit, the way they use scientific evidence in their content depends

on the expectations of the community they serve. In their interviews with us, 90% (n = 10) of

the creators mentioned they shared evidence-based content learned during the summit with

their communities. But many questioned if the evidence shared during the summit would be of

interest to their particular audience (“The topics were so varying, and none of them felt

completely aligned with what I talk about all the time.” Creator 9) Others wondered whether

injecting evidence into their content would change what their audience has come to expect

from them (“I don't really want to feel too clinical. So it's almost like bridging the gap between

feeling like it's too academic versus, you know, like comfy and familiar.” Creator 2) Many

creators noted that when sharing lived experience they have started to offer disclaimers and

use captions to provide additional context. Creator 8 said “You just need to be really thoughtful

about your disclaimers.”

The summit heightened creators’ sense of responsibility

The summit presented research on where different segments of the American population

receive health information, and the trust they put in these sources. Creators were shown data

revealing that 75% of Americans start their search for health information on the internet

(National Cancer Institute, 2018), that many people believe that the average person who has

done their research knows as much as a medical doctor, and that information shared on social

media platforms by those that they trust can have more weight than if shared by a medical

professional (Edelman, 2023).


<!-- Page 19 -->


In their interviews, many creators noted that the summit increased their awareness of the

impact that they can have on their audience. They reported that being more aware of how

much their audience may trust their content made them feel more responsible about creating

accurate content. Creator 2 commented: “They're gonna listen to me more than someone that's

maybe in that sterile clinical environment. And so that really, I think, was a big take home. For

me, it was like, wow, that means that I have a really big responsibility.” Some already had an

idea of their impact and the summit reinforced it, like Creator 10, who said “I think that the

impact to me before the summit was a little bit invisible, and arbitrary, like I knew, but not

really.”

This increased sense of responsibility drove creators to do more to ensure that their content is

accurate. For example, Creator 2 noted ”Now there's a lot of cross points that go into my

content, like when I do something, and I cross reference, is this education targeting anyone? Is it

something that could be misinterpreted? Is it something that could be harmful if they read it a

wrong way?” Some creators also began ensuring that they are using their channel to share

more information grounded in best practices, like Creator 4, who said “ I'm trying to be very,

very careful about how I speak to interventions that I tried that are no longer the best practice.”

The summit validated creators’ work and motivation

Being invited to the summit by a well-regarded public health academic institution validated

creators’ work and motivation to help others. For example, Creator 9 mentioned “ I think it just

validated in a lot of ways that it's a real job, being a writer and a mental health advocate is a

real thing.” Many found this validation particularly important given the history of stigma around

mental health conversations. In the words of Creator 4, “[The] creator summit about mental

health was revolutionary. I grew up in a world where you didn't say depression. And so to be

seen and recognized and invited by [summit organizer], as someone who speaks honestly about

this stuff that felt really powerful.” The summit also legitimized the initial motivation for getting

into mental health content creation: to help others. For example, Creator 5 noted “it makes me


<!-- Page 20 -->


even more proud of the work that I'm doing, I wake up with this, this drive to want to do more

meaningful work.”

For some, the in-person summit reinvigorated that work. The interviews revealed that four of

the creators were ready to stop creating content prior to the summit. Creator 11 put it this way:

“Before the summit, I was really struggling for new ideas, I was fairly burned out on it. And I just

figured, well, maybe I've said pretty much everything I know to say.” The same creator went on

to describe how being part of the summit reinvigorated them to keep going: “It gave me a fuel

to keep on pushing.”

The summit showed creators’ their power as public health communicators and their potential

for impacting health at scale

When asked how they perceive their role in public health before and after the summit, 10 out of

the 11 creators interviewed mentioned it was their first time seeing themselves as playing a role

in public health. As Creator 6 said, “I think that was a huge part, a huge frameshift for me.

Realizing like, Oh, I am a part of a public health system. And so that was a huge revelation for

me at the summit.” For many creators, this realization came with a stronger sense of

responsibility. Creator 7 put it this way: “I think the coolest thing about the creator summit was

recognizing we do play a role in public health. And there is responsibility with that.” Many

creators talked about how the summit helped them truly see how they can use their platforms

to contribute to public health. For example, Creator 10 said “I definitely see myself now more a

public health leader without that title, right. But that my content reaches thousands, sometimes

millions of people and is impacting the inner worlds and lives of those people. And so I really do

see myself as someone who contributes to the public health of the world, which is pretty crazy.”

The summit helped creators find much-needed community

Prior to the in-person creator summit in August 2023, all 11 creators interviewed attended a

series of virtual creator briefings in April 2023. When asked about the impact of the summit


<!-- Page 21 -->


versus the virtual briefings, the majority of creators (n=9) ascribed greater impact to the

summit, thanks to the community it created.

“The in person summit, I think took everything to the next level for me. So I think my

content did change some with the April sessions. But the in person sessions, especially

the one that stands out is, like, how to tell a story. And then also just connecting with

other creators in person, and even outside of the summit—that's been really, really

helpful.” (Creator 8)

Other words creators used to describe the transformative experience of the summit included

“game changer” (Creator 7), “powerful” (Creator 4), “impactful” (Creator 6), and “enhanced the

experience tenfold” (Creator 9).

The summit provided a safe space for the creators to meet like-minded individuals and build

trust. Creator 1 described it as “the environment where everybody was telling their stories and

everybody there was so emotionally intelligent that they could hold space for everybody that

was there.” Creator 3 described the environment as “caring” and “safe.” Creator 6 noted that “it

was nice to meet people who you could tell genuinely wanted to serve their communities and

serve their audiences and not just [build] a massive following.”

Because social media content creation can be an isolating process with specific challenges,

many creators noted that hence finding such a community of creators was transformative:

“The biggest thing was it showed me that I am part of a family. It can be a pretty

isolating experience to be a content creator. Because you know, I see other people

making mental health content, but I've never met them. And so it just kind of seems like

we're all out on islands, sending out flyers, and never, never having any effect.” (Creator

11)


<!-- Page 22 -->


The qualitative interviews revealed the many benefits creators saw from this summit-catalyzed

creator community, including sharing information, supporting each other emotionally and

professionally, gaining other perspectives, sustaining motivation, and co-creating content

together. Notably, the creator community has had a long tail, with many creators noting that

they get in touch with each other on a weekly basis, even 7-8 months after the summit. The

summit host also organized a number of ongoing supports—including monthly creator calls and

a creator group text–that creators say maintained their sense of community.

“One of the things that I really appreciate are the call to action calls every month, just

hearing what people are doing and hearing what the School of Public Health is still doing

to promote this work. It's just really a great opportunity that I hope to continue to be a

part of the community.” (Creator 5).

## Discussion

A previous study demonstrated that although exposure to mental health toolkits increased

creators’ promotion of evidence-based mental health information, adding virtual trainings on

mental health research and evidence-based content creation did not result in any further

statistically significant increase (Motta et. al, 2024). This follow-up study analyzed how creators

viewed the impact of participating in an in-person summit on mental health and evidence-based

content creation. In in-depth interviews, creators who attended the summit self-reported more

evidence-based content creation. Additionally, creators reported that participating in the

summit had an influence both on the way they perceive themselves and their content-creation,

even 7-8 months after the summit. Creators who attended the summit reported that they saw

themselves as having a role in spreading public health information. They reported that

participation increased their awareness of their impact and sense of responsibility, motivating

them to be more intentional in making content, whether it be by seeking a wider variety of

sources, adding disclaimers, and/or sharing accurate information.


<!-- Page 23 -->


Notably, despite the value the creators placed on obtaining evidence-based content support

from public health institutions, they are primarily interested in sharing information that they

think will be the most relevant to their audience. This suggests that public health institutions

looking to support creators’ work must do more than simply make evidence accessible; they

must also engage creators in meaningful ways, such as in-person workshops and seminars, that

help creators connect with the evidence their audiences are looking for.

In addition, creators reported feeling part of a valuable community after interacting with public

health, mental health, and health communication researchers and other creators, which

benefited them both personally and professionally. Creators retained this sense of community

many months after the summit, with them attending monthly calls with the Center for Health

Communication [blinded for review] and seeking each other’s help and advice on a regular basis

via text and other means.

Paired with previous results demonstrating that mental health toolkits designed for content

creators can increase the amount of evidence-based mental health content that creators share

(Motta et al, 2024), the results in the present study reveal that an in-person summit spread over

several days can impact self-reported motivation and evidence-based social media content

creation. Summit programming was reinforced with these mental health toolkits; and although

we have not yet studied attending post-in-person-summit content in the same depth, the

creators’ potential for impacting health at scale can concretely be measured by content

collaborations with mental health, public health, and health communication faculty that

emerged from the summit. Those include creator-researcher co-creation of content about how

improving indoor air quality can protect mental health (Harvard Healthy Buildings Program,

2023), a social media campaign that helped pass first state legislation limiting sale of diet pills

and muscle building supplements to kids (Speer & Austin, 2024), and a social media campaign

to recruit research-study subjects from populations normally under-represented in such studies

(Marciano, 2024).


<!-- Page 24 -->


Limitations

This research has three limitations worth noting. First, creator responses are self-reported and

may be subject to biases such as recall errors and social desirability. Second, we were not able

to interview all creators who attended the summit; it is possible that those who participated

experienced a greater benefit than those who were unable to be included in this study. Third,

the particular characteristics of this group of participants might limit generalization of the

results in at least two ways. First, the creation of safe space and trust necessary for community

building might have been easier with mental health creators, compared to other groups. And

second, one of the selection criteria of the creators to participate in the summit was to not

feature obvious red flags in their content, as per the selection criteria; this group of creators

might therefore be predisposed to consider the impact of their content.

## Conclusions

In the wake of calls from researchers advocating for interventions to engage a broader audience

in health communication (Lutkenhaus et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2022), we are the first academic

or public health institution that we are aware of to conduct an in-person health communication

intervention for social media content creators.

This study documents the wide-ranging impact of our intervention on creators’ self-reported

health communication beliefs and behaviors, including their sense of responsibility and content

creation strategies. It also stresses the importance of in-person training to develop a community

with fellow creators and the institution, which plays a crucial role in the sustained activation of

creators as health communication partners. The Center for Health Communication hopes to

hold future interventions with social media content creators in other verticals, such as climate,

to influence the other spheres of public health communication. And it plans to study the effect

on the health communication beliefs of the public health experts who attended the creator

summit and in some cases started collaborations with the creators they met there.
